title: Effect of moisture control on the mechanical recycling of a commercial PLA/PHB blend under laboratory and industrial conditions
abstract: Abstract Biodegradable polymers, particularly aliphatic biopolyesters, are increasingly employed as sustainable alternatives to conventional plastics; however, their practical implementation within circular material schemes critically depends on their ability to withstand repeated thermomechanical processing. Processing-induced degradation, strongly influenced by moisture, therefore represents a key materials science challenge for biodegradable polyesters intended for mechanical recycling. In this study, the mechanical recyclability of a commercial injection-molding-grade PLA/PHB blend was systematically investigated with a specific focus on moisture control as a technological parameter governing degradation pathways and processing stability. Mechanical recycling was evaluated under laboratory-simulated conditions using repeated extrusion with and without material pre-drying, as well as under realistic industrial conditions employing a closed-loop injection molding and regranulation process with controlled moisture management. Changes in molecular characteristics, rheological behavior, thermophysical properties, mechanical performance, and optical properties were monitored over multiple recycling cycles to distinguish between hydrolytic and thermomechanical degradation mechanisms. The results show that residual moisture decisively affects the initial degradation state of biodegradable polyesters during melt processing. Recycling without pre-drying led to pronounced hydrolytic chain scission already in the first processing steps, resulting in a significant reduction of molecular weight, decreased melt viscosity, increased scatter in mechanical properties, and more pronounced color changes. In contrast, pre-drying did not eliminate degradation during subsequent recycling cycles but preserved a higher initial molecular weight and melt viscosity, which were subsequently maintained throughout further processing. Consequently, dried materials exhibited improved processing stability, more consistent mechanical behavior, and enhanced optical stability. Notably, despite higher thermomechanical loading, industrially recycled samples retained stable molecular, rheological, and mechanical properties when effective moisture control was applied. The results indicate that moisture primarily governs the initial stage of degradation through hydrolytic chain scission, while subsequent property evolution is predominantly controlled by thermomechanical degradation processes once the molecular structure stabilizes. These findings demonstrate that biodegradable biopolyester-based materials, exemplified by the investigated PLA/PHB blend, can remain mechanically recyclable across multiple processing cycles. While recycling without drying offers an energetically favorable route for applications tolerant to moderate property variations, moisture control provides a clear technological advantage by stabilizing degradation pathways and widening the processing window. More broadly, this work highlights that biodegradability and mechanical recyclability are not mutually exclusive, and that controlled processing conditions enable biodegradable polyesters to be effectively integrated into circular material strategies.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Biodegradable polymers, particularly aliphatic polyesters, are increasingly considered as sustainable alternatives to conventional plastics in a wide range of applications. However, their broader industrial implementation is closely linked not only to their end-of-life behavior, but also to their stability during melt processing and repeated thermomechanical loading. In the case of polyester-based materials, residual moisture plays a critical role, as it can promote hydrolytic chain scission during processing, thereby affecting molecular structure, rheological behavior, and functional properties.

Plastics play a crucial role in modern society due to their versatility, low production costs, and broad processing possibilities, which have enabled their extensive use in packaging, automotive, construction, and consumer goods sectors [ 1 ,  2 ]. At the same time, the growing production of short-lived and single-use plastic products has led to the accumulation of plastic waste in landfills and the natural environment, highlighting the unsustainability of the current linear plastic economy [ 3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6 ].

Biodegradable polymers derived from renewable resources have therefore attracted increasing attention as potential alternatives to conventional fossil-based plastics [ 7 ]. These materials are capable of degrading through biological processes into low-molecular-weight products, with the rate and extent of degradation depending on environmental conditions such as temperature, humidity, oxygen availability, and microbial activity [ 8 ,  9 – 10 ]. However, biodegradability alone does not represent a comprehensive solution to plastic waste management, as degradation under real conditions is often slow, incomplete, or difficult to control [ 9 ,  10 ]. Consequently, European legislation prioritizes waste prevention, reuse, and recycling over energy recovery and landfilling [ 11 ,  12 ,  13 – 14 ].

From an environmental perspective, mechanical recycling is generally regarded as the most energy-efficient and environmentally favorable route for plastic waste management [ 15 ,  16 ]. Life cycle assessment studies confirm its potential to reduce energy consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and the demand for primary raw materials [ 17 ,  18 ]. However, biodegradable polyesters are particularly susceptible to thermomechanical, hydrolytic, and oxidative degradation during repeated processing, leading to chain scission and a gradual loss of molecular weight, viscosity, and mechanical performance. The degradation sensitivity of individual components in PLA/PHB systems is not identical. PLA is primarily susceptible to hydrolytic degradation through random chain scission of ester bonds, strongly accelerated by the presence of residual moisture, whereas PHB exhibits lower thermal stability and is more prone to thermally induced degradation during melt processing. As a result, the overall degradation behavior of PLA/PHB blends reflects the combined contribution of hydrolytic and thermomechanical mechanisms, depending on processing conditions and moisture content. [ 8 ,  15 ,  16 ,  19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 ,  23 – 24 ].

The recyclability of biodegradable polymers is further influenced by the presence of plasticizers, stabilizers, fillers, and compatibilizers commonly used in commercial formulations [ 25 ,  26 ,  27 ,  28 – 29 ]. During recycling, these components may affect degradation kinetics, phase morphology, and interfacial interactions, thereby modifying the properties of recycled materials [ 30 ,  31 ,  32 ,  33 ,  34 – 35 ]. Although the use of chain extenders and reactive compatibilizers can partially compensate for molecular weight loss and improve processing stability [ 36 ,  37 – 38 ], it increases formulation complexity and may not always be compatible with existing recycling streams or regulatory constraints [ 39 ,  40 – 41 ].

Among biodegradable polymers, polylactic acid (PLA) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are considered two of the most promising material families due to their renewable origin, biodegradability, and mechanical properties comparable to certain conventional plastics [ 42 ,  43 ]. PLA is a linear aliphatic polyester whose properties strongly depend on stereochemistry, molecular weight, and processing history [ 44 ,  45 ]. Polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), as the most prominent representative of PHAs, exhibits high stiffness and good barrier performance, but suffers from brittleness, a narrow processing window, and pronounced thermal instability, often becoming unprocessable after only a few processing cycles [ 46 ,  47 ,  48 ,  49 – 50 ].

Polymer blending has therefore been widely employed to overcome the intrinsic limitations of neat PLA and PHB [ 51 ,  52 ,  53 – 54 ]. PLA/PHB blends have demonstrated synergistic effects, including enhanced toughness, modified crystallization behavior, and improved thermomechanical stability. These synergistic effects are generally attributed to the combination of a more ductile amorphous PLA phase with a more crystalline and stiff PHB phase, resulting in a balance between toughness and stiffness, as well as modified crystallization behavior and phase morphology [ 44 ,  51 ,  55 ]. Their properties are strongly influenced by blend composition, molecular weight, processing conditions, and the presence of plasticizers or compatibilizers [ 52 ,  53 ]. As a result, PLA/PHB blends have been investigated for a wide range of applications, including packaging, agriculture, medical uses, and additive manufacturing [ 56 ,  57 ,  58 ,  59 – 60 ].

With the increasing market penetration of bioplastics, effective end-of-life strategies have become increasingly important [ 61 ,  62 – 63 ]. While industrial composting is often considered a suitable disposal route, its practical applicability is limited by insufficient infrastructure and strict processing requirements [ 61 ,  62 ]. Mechanical recycling is therefore increasingly recognized as a necessary component of circular economy approaches for biodegradable polymers, enabling material reuse and conservation of renewable resources [ 21 ,  22 ,  64 ].

Numerous studies have investigated the effect of repeated processing on neat PLA, neat PHB and PLA/PHB blends, mainly under laboratory-scale extrusion conditions or within additive manufacturing contexts [ 16 ,  18 ,  44 ,  45 ,  51 ,  57 ,  58 ,  65 ]. These studies consistently report progressive degradation manifested by decreasing molecular weight, viscosity, and ductility with increasing numbers of processing cycles. PHB has been shown to be particularly sensitive to repeated thermomechanical loading, whereas PLA/PHB blends generally exhibit improved reprocessability due to synergistic interactions between the two polymer components [ 50 ,  65 ].

A critical factor influencing the recyclability of biodegradable polyesters is residual moisture. Due to the susceptibility of ester bonds to hydrolytic cleavage, the presence of water during melt processing can significantly accelerate degradation, particularly during repeated recycling cycles [ 27 ,  31 ,  33 ]. Despite this, moisture control and pre-drying are often treated as secondary processing parameters rather than as key factors governing the environmental and technological efficiency of recycling processes. From an environmental standpoint, mandatory drying prior to each processing step represents an additional energy demand, raising the question of whether moisture control is a strict prerequisite for recycling or rather a technological optimization tool aimed at improving material quality and processing stability. However, a systematic understanding of the primary versus secondary role of moisture in governing degradation pathways during repeated mechanical recycling remains limited. In particular, direct comparisons of recycling with and without material pre-drying under both laboratory-simulated and industrial conditions are still scarce.

In this work, the mechanical recyclability of a commercial PLA/PHB blend is systematically investigated with a specific focus on the role of moisture during repeated thermomechanical processing. The material is recycled under controlled laboratory conditions, both with and without pre-drying, and the results are directly compared with recycling performed under realistic industrial closed-loop processing conditions. Changes in molecular characteristics, rheological behavior, thermal properties, mechanical performance, and color stability are analyzed to provide a comprehensive, materials-based assessment of processing stability and recyclability in biodegradable polyester systems.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: A biodegradable polymer blend based on polylactic acid (PLA), polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) and an oligomeric plasticizer was investigated in this study. The material was evaluated within two experimental frameworks corresponding to laboratory-scale and industrial-scale mechanical recycling, enabling a direct comparison between controlled laboratory conditions and realistic industrial processing.

For the laboratory recycling experiments, the PLA/PHB blend was prepared in-house using commercially available PLA, PHB and a suitable oligomeric plasticizer. The formulation was designed to closely match the target composition of the commercial injection-molding-grade material NONOILEN® IM 3056-2, particularly with respect to the PLA/PHB ratio and plasticizer content. According to the target formulation, the blend contained more than 10 wt% of PLA, more than 30 wt% of PHB and less than 15 wt% of plasticizer. The exact formulation is confidential and therefore not disclosed. This approach ensured that the laboratory-prepared material was representative of the commercial blend while allowing systematic investigation under controlled recycling conditions.

For the industrial recycling experiments, a commercially compounded biodegradable blend marketed under the trade name NONOILEN® IM 3056-2 was supplied in the form of ready-to-process granules by Panara, a.s. (Nitra, Slovak Republic). Industrial-scale processing and recycling were carried out in cooperation with the industrial partner Remarkplast, s.r.o. (Zlín, Czech Republic) using standard processing conditions applied in industrial practice for biodegradable polymer blends.

Both the laboratory-prepared and industrially compounded materials were based on the same polymer components and the same target composition. This ensured the relevance of the comparison between laboratory-simulated recycling and industrial closed-loop recycling routes.

The basic properties of the virgin commercial polymer blend NONOILEN® IM 3056-2, corresponding to the zero processing cycle, are summarized in Table  1 . sections.heading: Methods of sample preparation
paragraphs: The mechanical recycling of the investigated biodegradable PLA/PHB blend was performed under laboratory and industrial conditions using three distinct recycling routes. These routes were designed to systematically evaluate the influence of moisture control and processing conditions on the degradation behavior and property evolution of the material during repeated mechanical recycling.

The first recycling route represented laboratory-scale mechanical recycling without any material drying prior to processing. This scenario was selected as a reference case corresponding to repeated melt processing under conditions without moisture control and can be considered a worst-case scenario for hydrolytically sensitive polyester-based materials.

The second recycling route involved laboratory-scale mechanical recycling with controlled material drying applied prior to each processing cycle. This route enabled isolated assessment of the effect of moisture control on degradation behavior, processing stability, and property retention under otherwise identical thermomechanical conditions.

The third recycling route was based on industrial-scale mechanical recycling of a commercially compounded PLA/PHB blend and was designed to reflect realistic industrial practice. This route employed a closed-loop processing scheme combining injection molding of test specimens with mechanical regranulation and subsequent reuse of the recycled material. Material drying was applied in accordance with standard industrial procedures for moisture-sensitive biodegradable polyesters.

By comparing these three recycling routes, the experimental design allowed differentiation between the effects of repeated thermomechanical loading, moisture presence, and processing scale. This approach provided a comprehensive framework for evaluating environmentally and technologically balanced recycling strategies for biodegradable polymer blends.

sections.heading: Polymer blend preparation for study of mechanical recycling in laboratory conditions
paragraphs: The PLA/PHB polymer blend used for laboratory-scale mechanical recycling experiments was prepared in-house to obtain a material representative of the commercial injection-molding-grade blend NONOILEN® IM 3056-2. The laboratory-prepared blend was intended to serve as a model material enabling controlled investigation of the effects of repeated mechanical recycling and moisture control under well-defined processing conditions.

Compounding of the PLA/PHB blend was carried out using a co-rotating intermeshing twin-screw extruder (LabTech 16, LabTech Engineering, Thailand) with a screw diameter of 16 mm and a length-to-diameter (L/D) ratio of 40. The screw speed was set to 150 rpm. The temperature profile along the extruder barrel, from the feeding zone to the die, consisted of ten heating zones set to 60 °C, 140 °C, five zones at 190 °C, followed by 160 °C, 150 °C and 150 °C.

The compounded polymer melt was extruded through a strand die, cooled in a water bath, and subsequently pelletized to obtain granules suitable for further processing. This material, corresponding to the zero processing cycle (REC 0), was used as the starting material for subsequent laboratory-scale mechanical recycling experiments.

The preparation procedure ensured homogeneous distribution of the polymer components and the plasticizer within the blend, while minimizing uncontrolled degradation prior to the recycling experiments. All further recycling steps were performed using this laboratory-prepared material to allow systematic evaluation of degradation behavior induced exclusively by repeated processing and moisture control.

sections.heading: Material recycling in laboratory conditions by multiple extrusion
Study of material recycling of PLA/PHB blend under laboratory conditions without material drying
paragraphs: Laboratory-scale mechanical recycling without material drying was carried out using the laboratory-prepared PLA/PHB blend described in the previous section. This recycling route was selected as a reference scenario representing repeated melt processing without moisture control and can be considered a worst-case condition for hydrolytically sensitive polyester-based materials.

Mechanical recycling was simulated by subjecting the material to multiple consecutive extrusion cycles using a single-screw extruder (Plasticorder Brabender, Brabender GmbH and Co. KG, Duisburg, Germany). The extruder was equipped with a screw having a diameter of 19 mm, a length-to-diameter ( L / D ) ratio of 25 and a compression ratio of 1:3. A circular die with a diameter of 2 mm was used. The screw speed was set to 55 rpm, resulting in an average material residence time of approximately 58 s. The temperature profile along the extruder barrel, from the feeding zone to the die, was set to 170 °C, 185 °C, 190 °C and 180 °C.

During each processing cycle, the polymer melt was extruded through the die, cooled in a water bath, and subsequently pelletized to obtain granules. The resulting granulate was directly reused as feedstock for the subsequent extrusion cycle without any intermediate drying step. The material was processed through up to five consecutive recycling cycles. All extrusion parameters were kept constant for all recycling cycles to ensure that observed changes originated exclusively from material degradation effects.

After each recycling cycle, samples were collected and designated according to the number of processing cycles. The obtained materials were non-dried prior to further processing or characterization. This approach ensured that the influence of residual moisture on degradation behavior, processing stability, and property evolution could be systematically evaluated.

The materials obtained via this recycling route served as reference samples for comparison with laboratory recycling performed with controlled material drying and with industrial-scale recycling under realistic processing conditions.

sections.heading: Study of material recycling of PLA/PHB blend under laboratory conditions with prior drying of the material
paragraphs: Laboratory-scale mechanical recycling with prior material drying was performed using the same laboratory-prepared PLA/PHB blend and identical processing conditions as described for recycling without material drying. This recycling route was designed to assess the influence of moisture control on material behavior during repeated mechanical recycling.

Before each extrusion cycle, the granulated material was dried in a circulating-air oven at 70 °C until constant mass was reached which typically corresponds to a drying time of approximately 2.5–4 h depending on the sample batch. Drying to constant mass was applied to ensure comparable and reproducible moisture conditions prior to each processing cycle. After drying, the material was immediately processed to minimize moisture uptake from the ambient environment. The moisture content of the tested samples before drying is summarized in Table  2  and confirms the presence of significant residual moisture prior to processing. The moisture content reported for REC 0-D corresponds to the laboratory-prepared blend prior to the first recycling cycle. Table 2 Overview of laboratory-scale mechanical recycling routes of the PLA/PHB blend Samples without drying Sample name Extrusion number Processing Product REC 0-N 0 Twin-screw extruder (blending) Granulate REC 1-N 1 Single-screw extruder Granulate REC 2-N 2 Single-screw extruder Granulate REC 3-N 3 Single-screw extruder Granulate REC 4-N 4 Single-screw extruder Granulate REC 5-N 5 Single-screw extruder Granulate Samples with prior drying Sample name Extrusion number Processing Product Content of moisture before drying (wt. %) REC 0-D 0 Twin-screw extruder (blending) Granulate 1,05 REC 1-D 1 single-screw extruder Granulate 0,32 REC 2-D 2 Single-screw extruder Granulate 0,41 REC 3-D 3 Single-screw extruder Granulate 0,36 REC 4-D 4 Single-screw extruder Granulate 0,20 REC 5-D 5 Single-screw extruder Granulate 0,33 The symbol after sample name indicates drying of material before processing (N—not dried, D—dried)

Mechanical recycling was carried out by repeated single-screw extrusion using the same extruder configuration, screw geometry, temperature profile and screw speed as applied in the non-dried recycling route. After each processing cycle, the polymer melt was extruded, cooled in a water bath and pelletized. The resulting granulate was subjected to subsequent recycling cycles following the same drying–processing sequence. The material was processed through up to five consecutive recycling cycles. All processing parameters were kept constant for all recycling cycles to ensure that observed changes originated exclusively from material degradation effects.

After each processing cycle, samples were collected and labeled according to the number of recycling cycles. In contrast to the non-dried route, all materials obtained in this recycling route were dried to constant mass prior to further processing and characterization, enabling direct comparison between recycling routes with and without moisture control.

The process of mechanical recycling in laboratory conditions is shown in Fig.  1  and the designation of each studied sample is stated in Table  2 . Figure 1 Schematic representation of laboratory-scale mechanical recycling of the PLA/PHB blend:  a  repeated extrusion without material drying prior to processing,  b  repeated extrusion with material drying to constant mass applied before each processing cycle. In both routes, identical extrusion conditions were used, and the material was recycled through successive processing cycles (REC 1–REC 5).

sections.heading: Study of material recycling of NONOILEN® IM 3056–2 material in industrial conditions
paragraphs: Mechanical recycling of the commercial biodegradable polymer blend NONOILEN® IM 3056–2 under industrial conditions was carried out using a closed-loop processing scheme in cooperation with an industrial partner. This recycling route was designed to represent realistic industrial practice and to enable direct comparison with laboratory-scale recycling performed under controlled conditions.

The industrial recycling route consisted of successive processing cycles combining injection molding of test specimens with mechanical regranulation and reuse of the recycled material. Material drying was applied in accordance with standard industrial practice for moisture-sensitive biodegradable polyesters to ensure stable processing conditions. No formulation modifications, such as the addition of stabilizers or chain extenders, were introduced during recycling in order to reflect realistic industrial recycling conditions.

This industrial recycling route served as a reference for evaluating the transferability of laboratory findings to real processing conditions and for assessing the role of moisture control and processing scale in the mechanical recyclability of commercial PLA/PHB blends.

sections.heading: Material recycling in industrial conditions
paragraphs: Industrial mechanical recycling was carried out through repeated closed-loop processing cycles combining injection molding and mechanical regranulation. The experiments were performed using a commercially compounded biodegradable polymer blend NONOILEN® IM 3056-2, supplied by Panara, a.s., in cooperation with the industrial partner Remarkplast (Zlín, Czech Republic).

Virgin NONOILEN® IM 3056-2 granules (cycle 0) were first processed by injection molding to produce standard test specimens (dog-bone-shaped or paddle-shaped). After each injection molding cycle, the tested specimens were mechanically shredded and subsequently reprocessed by extrusion to obtain a regranulate. This regranulate served as the feedstock for the subsequent injection molding cycle.

In this way, the tested material was repeatedly subjected to combined thermomechanical loading induced by injection molding (specimen preparation) and twin-screw extrusion (regranulate preparation), thereby simulating material recycling under realistic industrial conditions.
Prior to each recycling cycle, the shredded material was dried in a hot-air oven at 70 °C for 4 h, in accordance with standard industrial practice for moisture-sensitive polyester-based materials.

Injection molding was performed using a Zhafir Venus II 400/80B FullElectric injection molding machine. The temperature profile from the hopper to the nozzle was 30–175–170–165–160 °C. The granulate was fed via a hopper, melted and injected into a double-cavity mold with a cold runner system. The mold temperature was maintained at 50 °C. During the holding (packing) phase, a pressure of 500 bar was applied for 10 s, followed by cooling of the molded parts in the closed mold for 20 s. After cooling, the mold was opened and the parts were removed.

Subsequent regranulation of the material was carried out using a twin-screw extruder (LabTech LTE 26) equipped with a vacuum degassing system. The barrel temperature profile ranged from 160 to 180 °C, the melt temperature was between 167 and 183 °C, and the screw speed was set to 200 rpm. The resulting regranulate was used as the feedstock for the next injection molding cycle.

Materials were collected after selected injection molding and regranulation cycles and designated according to the number of processing cycles and the applied processing route. These samples were used for comparison with laboratory-recycled materials processed with and without material drying. A schematic representation of the industrial recycling process is shown in Fig.  2 , and the designation of individual samples is summarized in Table  3 . Figure 2 Schematic representation of mechanical recycling of the commercial PLA/PHB blend NONOILEN® IM 3056–2 under industrial conditions. sections.heading: Experiments
paragraphs: The experimental program was designed to systematically evaluate the effects of repeated mechanical recycling and material moisture control on the degradation behavior and property evolution of PLA/PHB-based biodegradable blends. Materials recycled under laboratory conditions without drying and with controlled drying were directly compared with materials recycled under realistic industrial conditions.

Changes in molecular characteristics were analyzed to quantify degradation induced by repeated thermomechanical processing. Rheological measurements were employed to assess alterations in melt behavior and processability, while thermal analysis was used to investigate changes in thermal transitions and crystallization behavior. Mechanical testing was conducted to evaluate the retention of mechanical performance during successive recycling cycles.

The combined evaluation of molecular, rheological, thermal, and mechanical properties provided a comprehensive assessment of the mechanical recyclability of PLA/PHB blends under laboratory-simulated and industrial recycling conditions, with particular emphasis on the role of material drying.

sections.heading: Molecular characteristics
paragraphs: Molar mass of the tested material was determined by gel permeation chromatography. Measurements were performed by the Agilent Technologies 1100 Series instrument equipped with isocratic pump, and an autosampler. PL gel 5 μm mixed C column was tempered to 30 °C with chloroform as the eluent at the flow rate 1 ml/min. Linear polystyrene standards with narrow distribution were used to gain the calibration curve (10 points in calibration). Instrument was equipped with refractive index detector. 5 mg of sample was used for the measurement.

sections.heading: Processing (thermomechanical) stability
Thermophysical properties measurement
paragraphs: The differential scanning calorimetry (Mettler Toledo Inc. instrument) was used for the determination of basic thermophysical properties such as the glass transition temperature, the crystallization temperature, and the melting point of the crystallites. The heat difference required for heating by 1 K between the sample and the standard was measured. The standard in this case was an empty cup. Nitrogen was used as the inert gas, and the evaluation software was SW STARe. The conditions for measuring of thermal properties are summarized in Table  4 . sections.heading: Mechanical properties measurement
paragraphs: Mechanical properties of laboratory samples were measured by using the prepared strands from each extrusion cycle. The strands had a circular cross section with a diameter of 2,0 mm. Tensile strength at break ( σ b ) and the elongation at break ( ε b ) were determined according to ISO 527 standard by the Zwick machine at cross-head speed 1 mm/min in the deformation range of 0 -3%. When deformation reaches value 3% of elongation, the cross-head speed increased up to 50 mm/min.

The measurement of physico-mechanical properties of industrial samples was conducted by means of tensile testing according to standard procedures ČSN EN ISO 527-1 and ČSN EN ISO 527-2. For measuring of physico-mechanical properties dogbone-shaped specimens were used. The experiment was carried out on an Instron 3365 universal testing machine equipped with a 5 kN load cell and mechanical grips with a clamping force of 5 kN. A contact-type extensometer with a base length of 75 mm was utilized as the elongation indicator, attached directly to the gauge length of the specimen. Mechanical properties of the tested specimens were measured using at least five specimens for each material and processing condition.

sections.heading: Color changes measurement
Molecular characteristics
paragraphs: The molecular weight distribution curves (Fig.  3 ) provide detailed insight into the degradation processes occurring in PLA/PHB blends during mechanical recycling. A clear difference between dried and non-dried samples is already evident after material preparation. Non-dried samples exhibit molecular weight distributions systematically shifted toward lower values compared to dried samples, accompanied by a pronounced reduction of the high-molecular-weight fraction. This indicates preferential degradation of the longest polymer chains. This behavior can be explained by the higher probability of chain scission events occurring along longer macromolecules, which contain a greater number of susceptible ester bonds and therefore exhibit a higher likelihood of cleavage under both hydrolytic and thermomechanical conditions. Figure 3 Molecular weight distribution of the PLA/PHB blend after multiple recycling cycles under different processing conditions:  a : non-dried samples,  b : dried samples,  c : samples recycled under industrial conditions.

The absence of high-molecular-weight species in non-dried samples suggests rapid hydrolytic chain scission of ester bonds occurring already during material preparation or within the first processing cycle in the presence of residual moisture. In contrast, dried samples retain molecular weight distributions shifted toward higher values, with a more pronounced contribution of long polymer chains, consistent with suppressed hydrolytic degradation due to effective moisture control. These differences in distribution shape and position demonstrate that drying has a decisive impact on the initial molecular state of the material.

During subsequent recycling cycles, however, non-dried samples show only a relatively minor additional decrease in Mw with increasing number of processing steps. This behavior can be attributed to the fact that the most hydrolytically sensitive and longest polymer chains were already degraded in the initial stage, limiting further molecular weight reduction during recycling. As a result, the remaining polymer chains exhibit increased resistance to further chain scission, leading to a stabilization of the degradation rate during subsequent processing. This can be attributed to the reduced chain length and lower segmental stress in shorter macromolecules, as well as a decreased probability of further scission events.

In contrast, dried laboratory samples start from considerably higher Mw values and exhibit a gradual and controlled decrease in Mw with increasing number of processing cycles. In this stage, degradation is governed primarily by thermomechanical effects, while the influence of moisture becomes less pronounced. This confirms that the primary role of drying lies in stabilizing the initial molecular characteristics rather than in controlling degradation during later recycling cycles.

Industrially recycled samples exhibit a distinct behavior. Despite higher shear and thermomechanical stresses associated with industrial processing, dried industrial samples maintain nearly constant Mw values over successive recycling cycles. This indicates effective moisture control and stable processing conditions in industrial practice, which suppress hydrolytic degradation and ensure high molecular stability even under intensive processing.

The evolution of the polydispersity index (Ɖ, Fig.  4 B) correlates well with the molecular weight distribution results. Dried samples exhibit higher initial Ɖ values (approximately 2.5) prior to recycling, followed by a gradual decrease with increasing number of processing cycles. This trend reflects preferential scission of the longest polymer chains, leading to narrowing of the molecular weight distribution and progressive material homogenization.

Conversely, non-dried samples show lower initial Ɖ values (around 2) that remain nearly constant throughout subsequent recycling cycles. This stable Ɖ behavior indicates that hydrolytic degradation occurs relatively uniformly across the molecular weight distribution already during material preparation, resulting in a narrower and more stable distribution before recycling. The consistent evolution of Ɖ therefore directly supports the conclusions drawn from the molecular weight distribution curves and Mw trends.

Overall, the molecular characterization results demonstrate that drying has a decisive influence on the initial molecular characteristics of PLA/PHB blends, with the most pronounced effect occurring during material preparation. In later recycling cycles, degradation is governed mainly by thermomechanical loading, while the influence of moisture becomes secondary. Effective moisture control at early processing stages is therefore crucial for preserving high molecular weights and stable molecular weight distributions during mechanical recycling.

The observed molecular degradation trends are consistent with previously reported behavior of PLA-based materials and PLA/PHB blends during mechanical recycling, where molecular weight reduction is primarily attributed to hydrolytic and thermomechanical chain scission [ 16 ,  22 ,  35 ], [ 22 ,  35 ] Similar decreases in weight-average molecular weight upon repeated processing have been described for both neat PLA and PLA/PHB systems under laboratory conditions [ 24 ,  65 ].

In contrast to most literature studies treating drying as an implicit prerequisite, the present results indicate that drying mainly stabilizes the initial molecular characteristics by suppressing early stage hydrolytic degradation, while subsequent molecular weight evolution is governed predominantly by processing-induced thermomechanical effects. This finding is further supported by the high molecular stability observed for industrially recycled samples under controlled moisture conditions.

sections.heading: Processing stability
paragraphs: Processing stability of the recycled PLA/PHB blends was evaluated based on the dependence of complex viscosity and relative complex viscosity (Fig.  5 ) on the number of processing cycles for the individual recycling routes. The results demonstrate a close relationship between the rheological behavior of the melt, the molecular characteristics of the material, and the processing conditions, particularly moisture control and the intensity of thermomechanical loading. Figure 5 Dependence of complex viscosity  a  and relative complex viscosity  b  of the PLA/PHB blend on processing number in the 1st minute of the test for laboratory non-dried, laboratory dried, and industrially processed samples.

The first rheological plot (Fig.  5 A) shows that dried laboratory samples exhibit the highest initial values of complex viscosity prior to processing. In contrast, non-dried samples display significantly lower complex viscosity values already in the first processing cycle following material preparation. This difference is a direct consequence of moisture-induced hydrolytic degradation, which leads to rapid scission of polymer chains, particularly the longest macromolecules, resulting in a pronounced reduction in molecular weight. Across the entire investigated shear rate range, non-dried samples therefore consistently exhibit lower complex viscosity compared to dried materials, in agreement with the molecular weight distribution results.

Industrially recycled samples, on the other hand, exhibit the lowest initial values of complex viscosity. This behavior results from the substantially higher thermomechanical loading experienced by the material during industrial processing compared to laboratory conditions, leading to more intensive chain scission already at the initial processing stage. This apparent discrepancy reflects the fact that industrial processing induces a higher initial level of thermomechanical degradation, while effective moisture control leads to a stabilized molecular structure during subsequent processing cycles. Nevertheless, the decrease in complex viscosity of the industrial samples during subsequent processing cycles is relatively limited. Even after five successive processing cycles, the reduction in viscosity is not sufficiently pronounced to cause processing difficulties or to limit further material utilization. This observation indicates that, after drying, the material reaches a stabilized molecular state and maintains sufficient resistance to repeated thermomechanical loading.

The second rheological plot (Fig.  5 B), showing the evolution of relative complex viscosity with time, provides further insight into degradation kinetics. For all investigated materials, relative complex viscosity gradually increases with time, indicating a progressive decrease in the degradation rate during processing. This trend suggests that the longest and most degradation-sensitive macromolecular chains are preferentially cleaved during the initial stages of processing, while the remaining polymer population consists mainly of shorter and more stable chains. This leads to a progressive reduction in chain entanglement density and a simplified molecular architecture, which in turn lowers the probability of further chain scission and contributes to the observed stabilization of degradation kinetics.

As a result, the rate of molecular weight reduction, and consequently the decrease in complex viscosity, becomes progressively lower with increasing number of processing cycles. From a processing perspective, this behavior is favorable, as the material reaches a stabilized state after an initial adjustment of its molecular structure and can therefore withstand a higher number of processing cycles without a severe loss of rheological properties.

Overall, the rheological results confirm that the processing stability of PLA/PHB blends is closely linked to their molecular characteristics. Moisture and thermomechanical loading play a decisive role mainly in the early stages of processing, where they determine the initial level of molecular weight and complex viscosity. After stabilization of the molecular structure, further degradation is governed primarily by thermomechanical effects, while both dried laboratory and industrially recycled samples retain sufficient rheological stability for continued processing and practical application.

sections.heading: Thermophysical properties
paragraphs: The thermophysical properties of the recycled PLA/PHB blends were analyzed by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) in order to complement the molecular and rheological characterization and to assess the influence of repeated processing on thermal transitions. The glass transition temperature (Tg), melting temperature (Tm) and melting enthalpy of crystallites (ΔHₘ) were evaluated from the second heating cycle, thereby eliminating the influence of previous thermal history and enabling comparison of the intrinsic structural state of the materials.

The first DSC plot (Fig.  6 ) illustrates the evolution of the glass transition temperature ( T g ). Although  T g  does not show a systematic dependence on the number of processing cycles, small differences in absolute  T g  values can be observed between individual recycling routes. In particular, the highest  T g  values are observed for the blend recycled under industrial conditions. This behavior can be attributed to the distinct thermomechanical history associated with industrial processing, which may lead to a slightly more constrained amorphous phase. Such differences are likely related to variations in molecular weight, molecular weight distribution, and structural relaxation of the amorphous phase rather than to changes in chemical composition, which remains constant for all samples. At the same time, the limited variation in Tg indicates that the chain scission occurring during recycling does not fundamentally alter the nature of the amorphous phase but rather modifies its molecular relaxation only to a minor extent.

The second DSC plot (Fig.  7 A) presents the melting temperature ( T m ) of the crystalline phase. The melting temperature remains practically unchanged throughout repeated recycling and across all processing scenarios. This indicates that the crystalline structure of the PLA/PHB blend is preserved during both laboratory and industrial recycling and that thermomechanical degradation proceeds predominantly via chain scission without significantly affecting the stability or nature of the crystalline domains.

The third DSC plot (Fig.  7 B) shows the melting enthalpy of crystallites (Δ H ₘ), which provides indirect information on the degree of crystallinity. Changes in Δ H ₘ are generally minor for all recycling routes. While laboratory-recycled samples exhibit nearly constant Δ H ₘ values, a slight decrease in melting enthalpy is observed for industrially recycled materials. This effect may be associated with differences in crystallization efficiency or crystalline ordering resulting from the combined processing steps of injection molding and regranulation, which impose a more complex thermal and shear history on the material.

Overall, the DSC results confirm that the primary effects of repeated mechanical recycling and moisture control manifest mainly in molecular degradation and processing (rheological) stability, whereas the fundamental thermal transition temperatures of the PLA/PHB blend remain largely unaffected. The limited changes in  T g ,  T m  and Δ H ₘ demonstrate that the thermomechanical performance of the material is preserved even after multiple processing cycles, supporting its suitability for repeated mechanical recycling under both laboratory and industrial conditions.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties measurement
paragraphs: The results indicate that tensile strength at break ( σᵦ ) does not exhibit a pronounced systematic dependence on the number of processing cycles for any of the investigated recycling routes. This suggests that, despite progressive molecular degradation, the load-bearing capacity of the material remains relatively stable within the investigated range of recycling cycles. This behavior suggests that the remaining molecular network, although partially degraded, still provides sufficient chain entanglement and stress transfer capability to maintain the load-bearing performance of the material. However, clear differences in the absolute σᵦ values are observed between the different processing scenarios.

The highest σᵦ values (Fig.  8 A) throughout the experiment are achieved by the dried laboratory samples. This behavior can be attributed to their higher initial molecular weight and reduced hydrolytic degradation due to effective moisture removal prior to processing. Preservation of longer polymer chains promotes efficient stress transfer within the material, resulting in higher tensile strength.

Industrially recycled samples exhibit lower σᵦ values compared to the dried laboratory samples. This difference reflects the higher degree of molecular degradation induced by the more intensive thermomechanical loading typical of industrial processing, which involves repeated injection molding and regranulation steps. Nevertheless, σᵦ values of the industrial samples remain relatively stable over successive processing cycles and do not indicate a significant limitation for further processing or practical material utilization.

This reduction is associated with hydrolytic degradation initiated by residual moisture already during material preparation and the first processing cycle, leading to rapid scission of polymer chains and consequently to lower molecular weight and reduced mechanical integrity of the material. This trend is fully consistent with the molecular and rheological characterization results.

Elongation at break ( εᵦ , Fig.  8 B) exhibits a higher sensitivity to the processing scenario than tensile strength. The largest scatter in  εᵦ  values is observed for the non-dried samples, indicating increased variability in the mechanical response of the material. This behavior may be associated with differences in the degradation state induced by the presence of residual moisture during processing, which can result in a less homogeneous molecular structure and local variations in mechanical performance. Such heterogeneity can lead to localized stress concentrations and premature failure in weaker regions of the material, resulting in increased variability of elongation at break.

In contrast, both dried laboratory and industrial samples exhibit more stable and reproducible εᵦ values during repeated processing. This indicates a more homogeneous degradation behavior and better control of the structural state of the material, which is favorable from the perspective of mechanical reliability and processing consistency.

Overall, the mechanical performance reflects the combined effect of molecular degradation and structural stabilization, with moisture primarily influencing the initial degradation state and thermomechanical effects governing subsequent property evolution.

sections.heading: Color changes
paragraphs: The results show that color changes are strongly dependent on the processing scenario. Non-dried samples exhibit the lowest lightness ( L *, Fig.  9 A) values and simultaneously the highest total color difference ΔE (Fig.  9 B). This trend indicates more pronounced material darkening and stronger color changes already in the early stages of processing. In contrast, industrially processed samples exhibit the highest L* values and show better color stability over repeated processing cycles.

The observed changes in optical properties can be interpreted as a macroscopic manifestation of degradation processes occurring in the material. The increased color deviation observed for non-dried samples correlates well with the molecular and rheological characterization results, which demonstrated a pronounced reduction in molecular weight, the absence of high-molecular-weight fractions, and lower complex viscosity due to moisture-induced hydrolytic degradation. Therefore, color changes should not be considered an isolated phenomenon but rather a visual indicator of the overall degradation state of the material.

Despite higher thermomechanical loading, industrially recycled samples exhibit more favorable color stability. This behavior can be attributed to effective moisture control and a stabilized processing regime, which limit the extent of hydrolytic degradation and the associated changes in optical properties. These findings indicate that appropriately controlled industrial processing conditions can ensure not only stable mechanical and rheological properties but also preservation of a favorable visual appearance of the recycled material.

The observed color changes may be associated with the formation of degradation products commonly linked to polymer darkening during processing. However, in the absence of direct chemical analysis, these observations should be regarded as a correlation with the degradation state of the material rather than as direct evidence of specific degradation mechanisms.

Overall, the optical measurement results confirm that color represents a sensitive and easily observable indicator of the quality of recycled PLA/PHB blends. More pronounced color changes in non-dried samples reflect their higher degradation state, whereas dried laboratory and industrially recycled materials exhibit improved color stability. Optical properties thus effectively complement molecular, rheological, and mechanical characterization and support the conclusion that moisture control plays a key role in the mechanical recycling of PLA/PHB blends.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study systematically investigated the mechanical recyclability of a commercial injection-molding-grade PLA/PHB biodegradable blend under laboratory-simulated and industrial recycling conditions, with particular emphasis on the role of moisture as a governing processing parameter. By combining molecular, rheological, thermophysical, mechanical, and optical characterization, the degradation behavior and processing stability of the material during repeated thermomechanical recycling were comprehensively assessed.

The results demonstrate that the investigated PLA/PHB blend remains mechanically recyclable over multiple processing cycles under both laboratory and industrial conditions. Recycling without prior material drying was shown to be feasible, although it led to pronounced hydrolytic degradation already during the initial processing steps. This early stage degradation resulted in reduced molecular weight, lower melt viscosity, increased scatter in mechanical properties, and more pronounced color changes. Nevertheless, even under these worst-case conditions, the material retained sufficient processability and mechanical integrity for continued reuse, indicating a certain tolerance of the system to moisture-induced degradation.

Material pre-drying was found to provide a clear technological advantage by stabilizing the initial molecular characteristics of the blend. Although pre-drying did not prevent degradation during subsequent recycling cycles, it preserved a higher initial molecular weight and melt viscosity, which were subsequently maintained throughout further processing. As a result, dried materials exhibited improved processing stability, more consistent mechanical behavior, and enhanced optical stability. These findings indicate that moisture primarily governs the initial degradation state, whereas further property evolution is dominated by thermomechanical effects once the molecular structure has stabilized.

Importantly, industrial closed-loop recycling under controlled moisture conditions demonstrated that, despite higher cumulative thermomechanical loading, the PLA/PHB blend retains stable molecular, rheological, and mechanical properties across successive processing cycles. This confirms that the trends observed under laboratory conditions are transferable to realistic industrial processing scenarios and highlights the effectiveness of moisture control in maintaining processing robustness.

The obtained results further indicate that the degradation behavior of PLA/PHB blends during recycling follows a two-stage mechanism, where the initial decrease in molecular weight is primarily driven by hydrolytic degradation, while subsequent processing is characterized by a stabilized molecular structure with a reduced rate of further chain scission. This stabilization can be attributed to the prior degradation of the most susceptible high-molecular-weight fraction, which leads to a lower probability of further degradation in later processing cycles.

From a materials science perspective, the present results show that biodegradability and mechanical recyclability are not mutually exclusive. Mechanical recycling without drying represents an energetically favorable option for applications tolerant to moderate variations in material properties, whereas moisture control via pre-drying expands the processing window and enhances property consistency. Overall, the results provide practical insight into how moisture control influences processing stability and property retention during the mechanical recycling of biodegradable polyester blends.
